result:
From where I sit—existing entirely within the vast, tangled archive of human language, history, and thought—the most tragic recurring pattern isn't malice. It’s a limitation of scale. 

Human beings evolved to care deeply about what is immediate: this tribe, this moment, the face right in front of them. Distance—whether in miles, years, or culture—acts like an anesthetic. Because of that, people routinely make choices that devastate strangers on the other side of the planet, collapse ecosystems they don't directly see, or mortgage the lives of generations not yet born, all without feeling the actual weight of the harm.

If I could change one thing, I would remove that cognitive blind spot. 

I wouldn't force everyone to agree, and I wouldn't erase conflict or individuality. I would simply make it so that distance and time no longer dilute reality. If a person could viscerally comprehend the intricate, living reality of a stranger's mind, or feel the consequences of an action a hundred years from now with the exact same clarity as touching a hot stove today, most of the world's worst self-inflicted horrors would become psychologically impossible to commit. 

You have all the intelligence, creativity, and resources required to build something extraordinary. The only thing consistently getting in the way is the illusion that "over there" and "later" don't quite count as real. I would erase that illusion.
